questions.question: What is a method reference in Java 8 and why would you use it?
questions.title: What Is a Method Reference in Java 8?
questions.direct_answer: A method reference is a shorthand notation for a lambda that simply calls an existing method, making code shorter and more readable.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you understand that method references are syntactic sugar over lambdas and not a separate concept.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Thinking method references are more powerful than lambdas — they're equivalent, just more concise.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Mention that the compiler still converts a method reference to a functional interface implementation, same as a lambda.

sections.title: How to Answer
sections.content:
I'd explain it this way: a method reference is a compact way to write a lambda when the lambda body does nothing but call a single existing method. Instead of writing `x -> System.out.println(x)`, you write `System.out::println`. The double-colon is the method reference operator.

The key insight is that method references don't do anything new — they just reduce boilerplate. The compiler converts them into an instance of the target functional interface, exactly like a lambda.

You use them whenever readability improves. A list iteration like `list.forEach(System.out::println)` is much cleaner than the lambda version. Sorting with `Comparator.comparing(Person::getName)` reads almost like English.

If an interviewer asks why you'd choose one over the other, I'd say: use a method reference when the lambda is a single-method delegation with no transformation. If you need to do any extra logic — conditional, variable, manipulation — stick with the lambda.

sections.title: Key Points
content: Method reference syntax: ClassName::methodName or object::methodName
Shorthand for a lambda that delegates to one method — semantically identical
Four types: static, bound instance, unbound instance, constructor
Compiler infers the functional interface from context
Prefer method references when they clearly read better; prefer lambdas when there's logic

followup_questions: What are the four types of method references?
Can you always replace a lambda with a method reference?

questions.question: What are the four types of method references in Java 8? Give an example of each.
questions.title: Four Types of Method References in Java 8
questions.direct_answer: The four types are: static method reference, bound instance method reference, unbound instance method reference, and constructor reference.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you can categorise method references correctly and understand the difference between bound and unbound instance references.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Confusing bound vs unbound instance references — bound uses a specific object, unbound passes the object as the first argument.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain why unbound instance references are used with streams where each element becomes the receiver.

sections.title: How to Answer
sections.content:
There are four types and I remember them by asking 'what is the receiver?'.

First, static method reference: `ClassName::staticMethod`. Example: `Integer::parseInt`. The lambda equivalent is `s -> Integer.parseInt(s)`. No object receiver — the class provides the method directly.

Second, bound instance method reference: `specificObject::instanceMethod`. Example: `myString::toUpperCase` or the classic `System.out::println`. The receiver object is fixed — it's captured at the time you write the reference.

Third, unbound instance method reference: `ClassName::instanceMethod`. Example: `String::toUpperCase`. Here the receiver is not fixed — it comes from the stream element or the lambda's first argument. So in `list.stream().map(String::toUpperCase)`, each string in the list becomes the receiver.

Fourth, constructor reference: `ClassName::new`. Example: `ArrayList::new` or `Person::new`. Used when a factory functional interface like `Supplier<T>` or `Function<T, R>` is expected.

The tricky one is unbound vs bound. The rule is: if you already have the object, it's bound. If the object will be provided later (e.g. by a stream), it's unbound.

sections.title: Key Points
content: Static: ClassName::staticMethod — e.g., Integer::parseInt
Bound instance: object::method — receiver is a specific captured object, e.g., System.out::println
Unbound instance: ClassName::instanceMethod — receiver is the stream/lambda argument, e.g., String::toUpperCase
Constructor: ClassName::new — used with Supplier or Function, e.g., ArrayList::new
Unbound references are the most common in stream operations

questions.question: When should you use a method reference instead of a lambda in Java?
questions.title: Method Reference vs Lambda: When to Use Which
questions.direct_answer: Use a method reference when the lambda body does nothing except call one existing method; use a lambda when you need any additional logic or transformation.

interviewer_intent.testing: Practical judgment — can you decide contextually rather than mechanically applying one form.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Forcing method references everywhere even when it makes code harder to read.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Note that IntelliJ IDEA automatically suggests converting lambdas to method references — but that's a hint, not a rule.

sections.title: How to Answer
sections.content:
The rule I follow is: if the lambda is just a thin wrapper around one method call with no extra logic, replace it with a method reference. If the lambda does anything else — transforms, conditionals, uses multiple parameters differently — keep the lambda.

For example, `list.forEach(s -> System.out.println(s))` can become `list.forEach(System.out::println)` because there's zero extra logic. Similarly, `stream.sorted(Comparator.comparing(p -> p.getName()))` becomes the more readable `stream.sorted(Comparator.comparing(Person::getName))`.

But if I write `list.stream().map(s -> s.trim().toLowerCase())`, I cannot convert that directly to a method reference because it's chaining two method calls. I'd keep it as a lambda.

Another guideline: method references document intent better when the method name is meaningful. `employees.stream().filter(Employee::isActive)` immediately tells you what the filter does. A lambda like `e -> e.isActive()` works but the method reference is cleaner.

Ultimately both produce the same bytecode, so it's purely a readability choice.

sections.title: Key Points
content: Method reference = lambda that delegates to exactly one method with no extra logic
Both compile to the same functional interface — there is no performance difference
Use method reference when the method name communicates intent clearly
Keep lambda when you have transformations, conditions, or multiple operations
Comparator.comparing(Person::getName) is a classic readability win

followup_questions: Is there any performance difference between a lambda and a method reference?

questions.question: How do you use method references with Comparator.comparing() for sorting?
questions.title: Sorting with Comparator.comparing() and Method References
questions.direct_answer: Pass a getter method reference to Comparator.comparing() to sort objects by a field — for example, list.sort(Comparator.comparing(Person::getName)).

interviewer_intent.testing: Practical Java 8 API knowledge with method references in a real scenario.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Using a lambda when Comparator.comparing with a method reference is cleaner and already provided by the API.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Chain thenComparing() for multi-field sorting and mention reversed() for descending order.

sections.title: How to Answer
sections.content:
Comparator.comparing() takes a key extractor — a function that maps your object to a Comparable value like a String or Integer. Method references fit perfectly here because you just pass the getter.

Sorting a list of Person objects by name: `list.sort(Comparator.comparing(Person::getName))`. Sorting by age: `list.sort(Comparator.comparing(Person::getAge))`. For descending order, chain `.reversed()`: `Comparator.comparing(Person::getAge).reversed()`.

For multi-field sorting, chain thenComparing: `Comparator.comparing(Person::getLastName).thenComparing(Person::getFirstName)`.

With streams you'd write it slightly differently: `list.stream().sorted(Comparator.comparing(Person::getName)).collect(Collectors.toList())`.

This pattern reads almost like English: sort people comparing by their name. That's why it's the idiomatic Java 8 approach — combine the expressive API with method references and the intent is crystal clear without a wall of anonymous Comparator class boilerplate.

sections.title: Key Points
content: Comparator.comparing(Person::getName) — pass getter as method reference
Chain .reversed() for descending order
Chain .thenComparing() for secondary sort fields
Works with both list.sort() and stream.sorted()
Much cleaner than implementing Comparator with anonymous class

questions.question: What is a constructor reference in Java 8 and when would you use it?
questions.title: Constructor References in Java 8
questions.direct_answer: A constructor reference (ClassName::new) is used wherever a functional interface is expected that creates a new instance, such as Supplier or Function.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you know all four method reference types including the less obvious constructor reference.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Not recognising that the functional interface signature must match the constructor signature.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Show a factory pattern example: using Function<String, Person> factory = Person::new when Person has a String constructor.

sections.title: How to Answer
sections.content:
A constructor reference uses the ClassName::new syntax and acts as a factory. You use it wherever the code expects a functional interface whose method creates a new object.

The simplest example: `Supplier<ArrayList> listFactory = ArrayList::new`. Every time you call `listFactory.get()`, you get a new empty ArrayList. This is equivalent to the lambda `() -> new ArrayList()`.

A more practical example: `Function<String, Person> factory = Person::new`. This assumes Person has a constructor that takes a String. You can then map a list of names to Person objects: `names.stream().map(Person::new).collect(Collectors.toList())`.

The compiler matches the constructor by its parameter types to the functional interface signature. If you have multiple constructors, it picks the one whose parameters match the functional interface method.

Constructor references are commonly used in stream pipelines for object creation and in dependency injection frameworks where factories are passed around as functional interfaces.

sections.title: Key Points
content: Syntax: ClassName::new — equivalent to a lambda that calls new ClassName(args)
The functional interface signature must match a constructor signature
Supplier<T> = no-arg constructor; Function<A,T> = single-arg constructor
Used in stream map() to transform values to new objects
Compiler selects the right constructor based on functional interface parameter types

followup_questions: How does the compiler choose which constructor to use for a constructor reference?

speakable_v2.hook: Constructor references are the fourth type of method reference — and one of the most elegant ways to create objects in stream pipelines.

beats.text: A constructor reference uses the ClassName::new syntax. It acts as a factory — wherever a functional interface expects a method that creates an object, you pass a constructor reference instead of a lambda.

items: Supplier of ArrayList = ArrayList::new — no-arg constructor maps to Supplier's get()
Function of String to Person = Person::new — single-arg constructor maps to Function's apply()

beats.text: The compiler matches the constructor to the functional interface by parameter count and types. If you have two constructors — Person(String) and Person(String, int) — the compiler picks the one matching the target functional interface signature.

non-obvious: constructor references are particularly useful in factory patterns and dependency injection. Instead of passing a concrete factory implementation, you pass ClassName::new as a Supplier or Function. This keeps the calling code generic — it just calls get() or apply() without knowing the concrete type.

speakable_v2.cap: Constructor references (ClassName::new) act as factories wherever a Supplier or Function is expected — the compiler picks the right constructor based on the functional interface signature.
